You have some great suggestions already, let me add a few as a SF fan with a literary background.

The Left Hand of Darkness by Ursula Le Guin - won both Hugo and Nebula (the major SF awards) often used in literature studies courses. Has some pacing issues but is essential SF reading.

The Space Trilogy (Out of the Silent Planet, Perelandra, That Hideous Strength) by C.S. Lewis. Cosmology, theology, and philosophy wrapped in a Wells style space adventure.

The Handmaiden's Tale by Margaret Atwood. Alternative history view of totalitarianism, theocracy and feminism.

1984 by George Orwell. Required reading for everyone regardless of genre taste, full stop.

Slaughterhouse Five by Kurt Vonnegut. War novel? Time travel? Space adventure? Post modernist autobiograpy? Yes.

All of the above qualify as good literature that just happens to be science fiction as well.

Other suggestions:

Snow Crash by Neal Stephenson. Excellent virtual reality and near future romp. Diamond Age mentioned by others is a sort of sequel to this book, highly recommend reading this first.

Stranger in a Strange Land by R.A. Heinlein - So much of modern sci-fi uses this as a touchstone. It's not a perfect novel but it is probably the most influential and popular book by arguably the best golden age writer. Essential.

The Foundation Trilogy (Foundation, Foundation and Empire, Second Foundation) by Isaac Asimov - if there is a quintessential science fiction trilogy, this is it.

Anything by H.G. Wells.

That should keep you busy for a bit. Glad to answer other questions, to quote a long ago student I am obnoxiously well-read and not good at hiding it. 8)

The sci-fi genre contains every kind of story. Here is a sampling of books I've loved over the years.

For space opera, Charles Stross is a good contemporary writer. I liked Singularity Sky a lot.

Ernest Cline's Ready Player One is a gold mine of 80s nostalgia, and a great sci-fi story.

For more of Gibson's style, Mindplayers, by Pat Cadigan, is amazing. much better than Neuromancer, in my opinion.

And The Devil Will Drag You Under, by Jack L. Chalker, is great. I recommend Midnight At The Well Of Souls from him as well.

Clifford Simak's Way Station is a classic.

The Parable Of The Sower is one of the great post-apocalyptic books. World Made By Hand by James Howard Kunstler is in that genre too.

Larry Niven has been mentioned in this thread. I recommend Protector. Ringworld is flashier, but Protector is a better story, and better conveys the sci-fi aesthetic of the Space Age which has now passed.

F. Paul WIlson's The Tomb will introduce you to a character you'll really enjoy, Repairman Jack, who sort of has his own genre - "crime meets weird".

Agent Of Chaos by Norman Spinrad is a great sci-fi book that explores politics.

Empire Of The East by Fred Saberhagen is a great mingling of the sci-fi and the sword-and -sorcery styles.

Of course, you can't go wrong reading Philip K. Dick. Start with Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep, and see how much was left out of the movie Blade Runner.

Authors i always recommend are Robert A Heinlein, Isaac Asimov, HG Wells, HP Lovecraft, Ray Bradbury, Olaf Stapledon, and there are heaps more. I would also recommend looking at the list of Hugo and Nebula award winners and checking out some of those authors.

Flowers for Algernon: Intresting take on inteligence, contenedness, and social psychology.

Ender's Game: Young adult fiction, well thought out, overall enjoyable read.

Flatland: A fun exploration of dementional perception. The story is told by a 2-dementional being, explaining his experience to us 3rd demention folks. An exceptional way to start to understand the concept of dementions beyond human perception.

Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy: A zany take on space and multi-verse travel. Great sense of humor. I especially recomend the audiobook narrated by Stephen Fry.

A Canticle for Leibowitz: Post apocolyptic USA. The book covers well over 1000 years of future-history, and somehow makes it work well.

The Postman: Another post-apocolyptic story. Follows a man on his journey to survive, and understand his role in a badly damaged world.

You really can't go wrong with any of these books, and I believe that each of the above have an audiobook format available. I'd also recomend the general works of Robert A Heinlein, Isaac Asimov and Phillip K Dick for hard Sci-Fi fans.

Some inexpensive ones that are pretty good:

  1. Omega Force Series by Joshua Dalzelle: -- Romping space merc adventure with a rag-tag group of misfits set in our very own present day galaxy.

  2. Battlefront Twilight Company by Alexander Freed: -- Set in the star wars universe, traveling with front line soldiers in the fight against the Empire. Surprisingly gritty for the genre.

  3. Thrawn Trilogy by Timothy Zahn: -- Set in the star wars universe, ( okay, so I reaally liked star wars in high school. Bit biased there) this features an easy narrative to follow, and surprisingly, a more compelling set of "bad guys" than good.

  4. Black Fleet Trilogy by Joshua Dalzelle: -- The "unknown alien menace" trope has been beaten silly in the sci-fi world. Dalzelle manages to freshen up the genre with political intrigue, and truly jaw-dropping naval engagements.

  5. Play to Live series by D.Rus: -- In an emerging genre (the fully immersed online experience), D.Rus explores MMOs from one very simple question: "what if we could permanently live in one". The world unfolding around that premise is rich, humorous, sacrilegious, and suprisingly engaging philosophically.

  6. End Online by D. Wolfin: -- This is definitely a freshman effort. It lacks polish, is plot holed like swiss cheese, and at times made me want to hunt down and do bad things to its editor. However, it is the first tottering step of a promising author, and there are many little gems of brilliance shining in the rough. Once again, we are exploring the idea of an immersive MMO, where the main character must find struggle to make ends meet in reality. It's worth the time if you can forgive some inconsistencies.

  7. Foundation Series by Isacc Asimov: -- Words cannot. Of all the sci-fi series i've ever read, this one is mandatory. A treat for both the computer science and English major, Asimov uses the lense of the cosmos itself to examine human nature and technology, and our propensities as a species.

  8. Rama Series by Arthur C Clarke: -- If you find the Foundation Series to your liking, you might enjoy the Rama Series. You'll be following mankind through the sterile, yet compassionate eyes of alien observers, documenting and judging the fitness of the species to expand across the stars.

High fives everyone! Lots of great suggestions on this list.
